items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.rss_description: Pricing at the Speed of the Market Emerging Technologies RyanMeyer Wed, 10/28/2026 - 11:33 As loss costs shift and new risks emerge, modern insurance pricing platforms are shortening the path from insight to price and changing how pricing works with underwriting. November 11, 1111 Image Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Kumarappan Sundaram Pricing is moving from a periodic project to a continuous capability. With catastrophe volatility and shifting market conditions, treating pricing as an occasional exercise is hard to sustain. Two shifts stand out. First, dedicated pricing platforms. Rating, models and rules increasingly sit on purpose-built platforms rather than inside the core policy system. Second, modern software discipline. Version control, automated testing and continual monitoring of live models are becoming standard. Paul Carroll What is driving carriers to invest in sophisticated pricing platforms now? Kumarappan Sundaram Five things. First, speed-to-market of rate changes. Moving from quarterly or annual releases, gated by IT and policy admin deployment, to something near-continuous is the key value. Decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is also a practical starting point for core modernization, delivering value without an entire core replacement. Second, loss cost volatility and trend uncertainty. Social inflation, repair and parts costs, tariffs and secondary-peril catastrophe losses make trend assumptions go stale faster. Carriers want faster feedback from emerging claims experience that they can incorporate into price. Third, segment-level control. Carriers want to grow where they are well priced and hold the line where they are not, which means testing, deploying and monitoring changes at a granular level. Fourth, regulatory and governance demands. Filing, documentation and explainability requirements keep growing. Audit trails can be far easier to build in than to retrofit. Fifth, data ecosystem expansion. Telematics, geospatial and property-level data, cat model output and third-party enrichment should flow into rating at quote speed, which can often be the real integration challenge. A CFO will often ask how the benefit is measured, so programs should define measurement up front. Paul Carroll Underwriting and pricing are tightly linked conceptually, but loosely coupled in practice. Why is that, and can they be brought into phase? Kumarappan Sundaram The link is strong in theory but weak in practice, mainly for technology and operating-model reasons. Start with systems and data. Pricing logic sits in a rating engine or pricing platform, while underwriters work in a different workbench based on the data in the submission, so the two rarely share a view of the risk. Then there are different rhythms. Pricing changes on a release cycle, while underwriting decisions are made submission by submission. Overrides and discounts help fill the gap. Finally, the feedback loop is weak. Why underwriters override a price rarely flows back to pricing in a structured way, so a valuable signal is lost. Modern pricing platforms increasingly aim to close this gap. Bringing them into phase is mainly an integration and governance task. Pricing can be exposed as a service that the underwriting workbench calls in real time, connected to appetite, distribution, retention and claims signals. Overrides can be captured as data, and authority and guardrails can be made explicit. In complex commercial risks, underwriter judgment legitimately plays a larger role, so the aim there is visibility and learning, not automation. Paul Carroll How can modern pricing technology help carriers price emerging risks? Kumarappan Sundaram Emerging risks, such as cyber, climate-related perils and new auto and energy technologies, may not come with deep loss history. A modern platform helps in four ways. First, new data sources as proxies. Outside-in cyber scans, geospatial and property-level data, and vehicle and telematics data give carriers signals where claims history is thin. The platform brings them together with internal experience and subject matter specialist judgment, with clear rules for how the weighting shifts as claims data builds. Second, scenario testing. Teams can test prices against stress scenarios, such as a major catastrophe or a systemic cyber event. Third, fast, controlled learning. Small, measured changes show what a new risk is worth sooner and with less exposure than a book-wide change. Fourth, flexible product design. Configurable rating makes it easier to adjust deductibles, sublimits and endorsements as understanding of the risk develops. The limit can be that technology cannot create data that does not exist. For novel risks, the platform helps carriers learn and adjust quickly, alongside accumulation controls, reinsurance and underwriting oversight. Paul Carroll What impact is AI having on pricing and rating, and where should leaders be skeptical? Kumarappan Sundaram I would separate what is emerging with clear value from what is still unproven. The clearest near-term value is GenAI around the pricing process. The more underrated opportunity is in the work surrounding the price: drafting and reconciling rate filings, translating pricing specifications into platform configuration, documenting changes, summarizing competitor filings and preparing data. These steps slow the path to market, and errors are easier to review than in a pricing decision itself. What is still unproven is AI acting on pricing decisions. The idea of agents that monitor performance, propose rate actions and test them is compelling. But pricing is regulated and auditable, and many carriers are not ready for autonomous rate changes. For now, I expect AI to propose and people to approve, so the quality of that review is the real control. As AI capabilities become widely available, proprietary data, speed of deployment and governance are likely to matter more as differentiators. Carriers that treat AI as a standalone upgrade, without the platform and operating model underneath it, risk building capability they cannot put into production. Paul Carroll What would you advise a carrier to do first? Kumarappan Sundaram Measure your cycle time, from the point a pricing change is approved to the point it is live throughout the various channels. Many carriers have never seen that number, and it shows where value is being lost. Then prioritize platform and process changes that shorten it. Put governance in place before scaling AI, and start with one or two lines where faster pricing has a clear, measurable payoff. Resist modernizing everything at once. Paul Carroll Thanks. This is all super helpful. -- Kumarappan (Kumar) Sundaram is a Managing Director in PwC’s Property and Casualty Operations and Technology practice and a leader of its Insurance Core Transformation and Pricing/Rating offering. With more than two decades of consulting experience, he partners with US and UK P&C carriers, from large international insurers to small regional ones, across personal, commercial, and specialty lines, with depth in commercial and specialty. He has led numerous large-scale programs modernizing policy, claims, and pricing/rating operations, and works with PwC’s strategy, management, technology, and actuarial teams to deliver integrated solutions, thought leadership, and sales. -- Sponsored by PwC Insurance Thought Leadership ITL Partner: PwC

items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.original_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.original_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

items.extracted_text: Hamilton secures upsized $300m Easton Re 2027-1 cat bond at reduced pricing - Artemis.bm Hamilton secures upsized $300m Easton Re 2027-1 cat bond at reduced pricing - Artemis.bm Hamilton secures upsized $300m Easton Re 2027-1 cat bond at reduced pricing 3rd November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Hamilton Insurance Group has secured its largest catastrophe bond yet, as the Easton Re Ltd. (Series 2027-1) deal has now been priced to provide an upsized $300 million of collateralized multi-peril retrocessional reinsurance protection, getting the capital markets coverage at a pricing level below initial guidance, Artemis understands. Hamilton Insurance Group, came back to the catastrophe bond market last month, for what will now become the third 144A catastrophe bond offering under the Easton Re name for the company’s reinsurance entity Hamilton Re . As we’ve explained before, Hamilton’s $200 million Easton Re Ltd. (Series 2024-1) cat bond is scheduled to mature early next year, which therefore makes this new offering appear to be a renewal of sorts and a meaningful upsizing of that coverage. Initially, the target was to secure $250 million of collateralized multi-peril retrocessional reinsurance to protect Hamilton. We then reported in a first update on this Easton Re Series 2027-1 deal, that the target size was raised to $300 million, while at the same time the price guidance on the notes was also lowered. We’ve now learned from sources that the notes have been successfully priced to secure the upsized $300 million of collateralized multi-peril retrocession priced towards the mid-end of the revised guidance. We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so be sure to visit Artemis’ Deal Directory entry for more background on the transaction . The now confirmed as $300 million Class A tranche of Series 2027-1 notes that Bermuda based special purpose insurer (SPI) Easton Re Ltd. is set to issue will provide Hamilton Re and Hamilton subsidiaries with industry-loss trigger and per-occurrence retro protection against U.S., DC, Puerto Rico, and Virgin Islands named storms, as well as U.S. and Canada earthquakes, over a three-year term. The $300 million of Series 2027-1 Class A notes from Easton Re come with an initial expected loss of 2.66%. Initially, these notes were first offered to cat bond investors with spread price guidance in a range from 4.75% to 5.25%, which was then lowered to a revised range of 4% to 4.75%. We’re now told the $300 million of notes have been priced to pay investors an initial risk interest spread of 4.25%, so below the initial guidance but not quite at the lowest end of the revised range. Hamilton has maximized its opportunity to increase its retrocessional reinsurance protection from the capital markets with this latest deal, as the company has successfully managed to capitalise on the strong demand being seen from cat bond investors across the market, while also securing the coverage at attractive pricing. items.extracted_text: Banks Start Reviewing Loan Terms for Clients in El Niño’s Path Article 0 Comments Banks whose clients are exposed to the super El Niño cycle building in the Pacific Ocean are now assessing loan structures and loss risks, with debt rescheduling among options being considered. Spain’s Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria SA, which aside from its presence in Iberia also has a significant client base across Peru, Argentina and Colombia, has asked local risk teams to conduct reviews of loan books as El Niño combines with global warming to pose a unique set of threats. Measures that can be considered by the bank for its most vulnerable customers include debt rescheduling, BBVA said in an analysis shared with Bloomberg. “The data we are currently generating supports this management process,” it said. Related: Money Managers Say There’s Nowhere to Hide as Super El Niño Forms Once BBVA is comfortable with its analysis, it will share the information with clients as part of its advisory process, it said. The climate phenomenon associated with warming across the equatorial Pacific Ocean is already fanning crop-damaging droughts and floods. The World Meteorological Organization says Southern Africa and Southeast Asia face heightened risks, while parts of Latin America are vulnerable to both drought and flooding. Concerns among banks follow warnings from money managers that the intensity of the current El Niño cycle will leave investors nowhere to hide, as the weather phenomenon disrupts commodities supplies, drives inflation and widens trade deficits. Banks based in the European Union are under particular regulatory pressure to report such risks due to evolving disclosure requirements under the EU’s so-called Pillar 3 rules, said Grace Osborne, a sustainable finance analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. She sees a heightened risk of banks needing to resort to “agricultural loan repayment holidays following severe climate events, given the insurance protection gap in European agriculture.” Danske Bank A/S, meanwhile, has warned of the implications of El Niño beyond commodities exposures. Companies headquartered outside geographic regions in El Niño’s immediate path may still be at risk via supply lines, with Danske citing shipping and logistics as examples of sectors in the crosshairs, irrespective of domicile. At JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Citigroup Inc., analysts have published research linking El Niño to heightened risks stemming not just from the agriculture, commodities and energy sectors, but from the impact on the broader economy. And Sebastian Werner, head of climate risk scenario design at Citi, cautions that a widely followed measure of El Niño strength — the Oceanic Niño Index, which focuses on the central tropical Pacific — doesn’t “capture all aspects” of the weather cycle, adding to the complexity of risk modeling. Banks already highlighting such exposures include Lima-based Credicorp Ltd., which estimated in August that some 9% of its loan book is directly exposed to clients at risk from the fallout of El Niño. The same month, Banco do Brasil SA Chief Financial Officer Marco Geovanne Tobias da Silva said the lender is “very concerned” and “closely monitoring the effects of El Niño,” during a call with analysts. Intercorp Financial Services, one of Peru’s biggest financial firms, says it has already set up special El Niño loan clauses for customers in fishing and agriculture, with the palette of instruments available including grace periods and reschedulings. Santander has 1.7 billion of agriculture, forestry and fishing loans exposed to physical risk. At Standard Chartered Plc, which aside from its operations in the U.K. also has significant client exposures in Africa, the Middle East and Asia, bankers are being asked to do a granular assessment of the risks associated with the current El Niño cycle. “We are closely monitoring the potential impacts of El Niño,” said Karen Wilkinson, global head of climate, sustainability and reputational risk at Standard Chartered. “We have undertaken analysis at a portfolio level across our corporate and investment banking business and are now incorporating this into client-level climate risk assessments.” That’s in addition to monitoring El Niño-related physical risks such as flooding, storms and heat stress, “across key operating locations and data centers,” she said. BI’s analysis of EU banks indicates that aside from BBVA, CaixaBank SA and Banco Santander SA also have agricultural loan books that are highly exposed to physical risks. Such exposures have the potential to feed through to credit quality faster than real estate loans, Osborne said. Julia Lucena, CaixaBank’s climate risk manager, said that “while sensitive exposures represent around 60% of the bank’s lending to agriculture, livestock farming, and fishing, the sector itself accounts for less than 1% of CaixaBank’s total lending portfolio,” in a written response to questions. “As a result, the sector’s overall physical risk exposure to the bank is considered limited.” CaixaBank said it monitors its lending exposure to physical climate risks across all sectors and has developed a framework to assess how weather events can impact credit risk metrics, especially the possibility of default, or of loss in case of default. Lending deemed sensitive to physical climate risks has remained relatively stable at the bank since 2022, Lucena said. Santander assesses climate risks under different scenarios and time horizons, including specific impact assessments when significant events take place, a spokesperson for the bank said by email. Santander has €1.7 billion of agriculture, forestry and fishing loans exposed to physical risk, equivalent to 56% of this portfolio. “Our current focus is on anticipation, preparedness and response capacity,” Santander said. The bank also has specific monitoring and early-warning mechanisms in place, including weekly weather bulletins and monthly El Niño updates, it said. “These help relevant teams identify potentially affected areas and assess exposure across portfolios and clients,” Santander said. The bank has “contingency and coordination procedures that can be activated” as needed, it added. BBVA said it expects to monitor the fallout of El Niño for its clients in two ways. What it describes as Phase 1 would entail quantitative analyses based on historical data, comparing neutral climate scenarios with the most intense El Niño events on record. Phase 2 entails integrating seasonal meteorological models with monthly updates for key variables to establish an early warning system to help clients prepare for extreme weather shocks. “This type of application has never been attempted before,” the bank said. “Therefore, it serves as a test and validation of the models for future use cases.” Top photo: A Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria SA (BBVA) bank branch in Barcelona, Spain, on Tuesday, June 24, 2025. items.extracted_text: AXIS Capital's third-party capital partner fee income continues to rise - Artemis.bm AXIS Capital's third-party capital partner fee income continues to rise - Artemis.bm AXIS Capital’s third-party capital partner fee income continues to rise 3rd November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans AXIS Capital, the global specialty insurance and reinsurance underwriter, has seen the fee income it earns through third-party strategic capital partner arrangements continue to rise in the third-quarter of 2026, with insurance-linked securities, quota share and the new Capacity Solutions division all contributing. Recall that, in 2025 AXIS Capital benefitted from leveraging alternative capital through partnerships with third-party investors, with these activities generating $54 million of ILS style fee income for the company last year . Then, in the first-quarter of 2026 , AXIS Capital reported a year-on-year increase in strategic capital partner fee income, which reached $23 million, up from $16 million in the prior year period. In the second-quarter of 2026 , AXIS reported that fee income from third-party capital partner initiatives rose again to $22 million, compared to $20 million in the prior year. Now, for the third-quarter of 2026, AXIS Capital reported that fee income from its so-called strategic capital partner activities reached $23 million, up from $19 million in the prior year. For the first nine months of 2026 the fee income figure reached $67 million, compared to $55 million for the nine months ended September 30th 2025. There’s been a steady increase every quarter for the last year or so now, as AXIS Capital has expanded activities with third-party capital providers. One source of fee income is AXIS’ partnership with insurance sector focused investor Stone Point on the casualty sidecar structure Monarch Point Re launched in 2023 , after a more than $400 million capital raise. AXIS has continued to launch new underwriting entities to support Monarch Point Re, the most recent being collateralized insurer Monarch Point Re (ISA 2026) Ltd. launched for the current underwriting year . AXIS reported the carrying value of its investment in the Monarch Point Re casualty sidecar like structure as having increased to almost $82.7 million as of September 30th 2026, up from almost $77.4 million at June 30th and almost $73.3 million at the end of March. Which does suggest the Monarch Point Re sidecar is proving profitable for AXIS, as its equity stake valuation continued to increase, which likely suggests attractive returns for Stone Point as the investor behind the structure as well. In Q3 2026, of the $23 million, of third-party capital feel income earned, $18 million was recognised by AXIS as a reimbursement of general and administrative expenses in its reporting. The company said the increased fee income is helping to drive down the G&A expense ratio, a trend which has now been visible over a number of quarters as the ILS and third-party capital activities benefit the company’s financial results. Once again this quarter, the AXIS Capacity Solutions business unit, which began operating in 2025 , is also mentioned as a fee income driver. AXIS Capacity Solutions works to develop structured and multi-line portfolio solutions at scale for capital partners, which is one way AXIS has been increasing its use of alternative capital to grow its business. After the first-half of 2026, the AXIS Capacity Solutions division was reported to have contributed $338 million of gross written premium, with the company saying this new reinsurance capital helps optimise its net exposure and lower its balance-sheet volatility. Now, after the third-quarter, the premium contribution to growth from AXIS Capacity Solutions has risen to $449 million, from open brokerage and selective delegated opportunities. The company continues to expect $17 million of full-year fee income from the Capacity Solutions activities. During the AXIS Capital third-quarter 2026 earnings call, CEO Vince Tizzio commented, “Through our AXIS Capacity Solutions capability, also known as ACS, we are matching our specialty underwriting knowledge with third-party capital. This is enabling us to serve clients with greater capacity while generating fee income for AXIS.” CFO Matthew Kirk further stated on third-party capital activities at AXIS, “Fee income in the quarter was $23 million, including $18 million, which served as an offset to G&A expense, and $5 million reported as other insurance-related income. This compares to $19 million of fee income in the prior year quarter. Note that the G&A offset derives from ILS vehicles and ACS-related fee income.” Utilising third-party capital within the business has been a driver of income for AXIS Capital and as one of the first-movers in areas such as casualty reinsurance sidecar structures the firm is well-positioned to continue finding new ways to harness investor capital within its business. items.extracted_text: Barclays Steps Up Client Reviews to Track Flood Exposure Article 0 Comments Barclays Plc has been stepping up its review process to ensure it detects client exposures to intensifying flood risks. The bank has been running internal models to make sure it’s tracking different scenarios, said Amit Puri, its head of sustainability for business. “You essentially get a higher level of review on some of these areas where there is potential for there to be a higher flood risk.” The process has developed over the past couple of years as Barclays reacts to the increasingly pronounced threat of flooding, Puri said. There is also growing anxiety in the UK about the availability of insurance for properties at risk of flooding. Last year, the Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority unveiled guidelines adding to pressure on banks to conduct closer analyses of flood, storm and other climate-related risks. Read more: England Has 1.2 Million Buildings at Risk of Flooding With No Defenses Barclays on Tuesday published a survey of UK business leaders, which showed that 86% have already had difficulty obtaining climate-risk insurance. At the same time, half those surveyed have directed capital away from areas perceived to be at higher risk of extreme weather shocks, while roughly one in 10 said climate change has played a role in decisions to close down or scale back business in the past five years. Over 40% of businesses in real estate and housing said they’d reallocated investment to focus on resilience to extreme weather instead of on cutting emissions. More than half those surveyed in those sectors said they’d invest in resilience if they had more information about how this might help their business. Across all businesses, flood risk was the top climate factor in determining the appeal of a location. Banks in the UK are under growing pressure to demonstrate they understand the risks posed by climate change, particularly with regard to flooding. A reinsurance program, Flood Re, currently allows customers with homes at high risk of flooding to obtain affordable insurance, but it’s set to end in 2039 and doesn’t cover homes built after 2009. The urgency of allocating capital to protecting assets from the physical fallout of climate change is growing, Puri said. “We were always aware of it, but we didn’t necessarily think it would happen until quite some time in the future,” he said. “Those physical risks that we used to think about academically maybe in 2017, 2018 are starting to materialize a lot sooner.” Barclays surveyed leaders of 700 mid-sized, large and very large businesses in the UK. The research covered sectors including agriculture, hospitality, manufacturing, housing and transport. items.rss_title: UK Cyber Chief Warns Firms ‘Willfully Blind’ to Hacking Risk

items.extracted_text: UK Cyber Chief Warns Firms ‘Willfully Blind’ to Hacking Risk Article 0 Comments The U.K.’s cybersecurity chief warned that Britain faces what could prove to be an unprecedented increase cyberattacks in the coming months and urged “willfully blind” businesses to come to terms with the risk. Richard Horne, head of the National Cyber Security Center, delivered the stark message to firms in a speech on Tuesday in which he said the country was at a “sliding doors” moment as threats from Russia, Iran and China rise. “In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyberincidents,” he said. “Far too many of our organizations and supply chains rest on weak technology and operational foundations.” Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply “When food isn’t on the shelves, when lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under, we may have to explain that we saw the warning signs, understood the risks and still didn’t make the right choices. Why we remained willfully blind,” he said. The warning comes amid a raft of high-profile cyberattacks and growing concerns that artificial intelligence tools are accelerating the cat-and-mouse game between hackers and their targets. Supermarkets across Europe were hit by suspected cyberattacks that resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers on Monday, with a small number of British firms affected, according to Horne, following a similar issue last month in France. In his speech, Horne accused Russia of working “every day” to attempt to penetrate Britain’s military networks, and said Iran was carrying out “malicious cyber operations globally including against the U.K.” The British chief chief said that China posed the most serious challenge to Britain, assessing that Beijing “highly likely has the intent and is best positioned to use AI for operations against our critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets.” China represented “the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge the U.K. faces,” he said. items.rss_title: APCIA Says Claims Data Standards in Works to Better Combat Criticism
items.rss_description: These days the insurance industry is “caught in the crosshairs,” and it may also be caught flatfooted – responding to recent questions of a policy’s worth rather than working from in front with appropriate data. In Boston at the American …
items.extracted_text: APCIA Says Claims Data Standards in Works to Better Combat Criticism Article 0 Comments These days the insurance industry is “caught in the crosshairs,” and it may also be caught flatfooted – responding to recent questions of a policy’s worth rather than working from in front with appropriate data. In Boston at the American Property Casualty Insurance Association (APCIA)’s annual meeting, board chair David Bell said the industry has succumbed to what has been dubbed the “horseshow effect.” “The far left and the far right have come together in this horseshoe effect,” he told the record number of registrants at the conference on the even of midterm elections. “We find ourselves at the intersection of left and right wing populism, where complicated questions like what percentage of claims are denied without payment are reduced to [make the industry] easy villains. Outrage can travel faster than truth.” David Bell speaking at the APCIA annual meeting in Boston. Bell, president and CEO of ALPS Corp., referenced recent reports from the Wall Street Journal on auto and homeowners claims . The publication said its analysis found an alarming amount of claims go unpaid. Two senators followed up the reports by sending letters to some of the largest insurers, asking for claims data. Related: Warren, Hawley Press Insurers Over Closed, Unpaid Claims | Industry Reacts to Senators’ Letter for Claims Data and Recent Reports “When provocative headlines suggest that getting an insurance claim paid is essentially a coin flip, our industry must be able to respond with clear, credible and unambiguous facts,” Bell said. “Claims are closed without payment for a variety of reasons other than a coverage denial.” However, the industry isn’t prepared to swiftly respond because it does not have consistent definitions and standardized coding to prevent different outcomes from being grouped together in an alarming headline-grabbing statistic. Bell said APCIA is developing a standardized claims-closed data-call template. “If we do not bring consistency to how claim outcomes are categorized, then we will remain on the defensive against narratives that the underlying data simply does not support,” he said. However, to add credibility, the industry must acknowledge when its members do not meet standards, he added. Bell said, “Defending the industry does not mean defending every action taken within the industry, including companies both inside and outside our trade organization. “When conduct falls short, we need to call it what it is. Otherwise, we risk sacrificing the credibility we need when the industry is being scrutinized unfairly.” He said APCI is working to bring consensus to defining clear expectations. “That way we can give vigorous defense to what is right without appearing to excuse what is not,” Bell said. items.extracted_text: UK Vehicle Production Rises Sharply in September Against Cyber-Hit Comparison Article 0 Comments Britain’s vehicle production rose sharply in September, industry data showed on Thursday, rebounding from a cyber-incident-hit comparison a year earlier. U.K. vehicle output increased 36.3% to 74,031 units in September, the strongest growth since August 2022, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) said. The increase reflected disruptions caused by a cyber incident at Britain’s largest automotive employer last year. Car production climbed 38.6% to 70,831 units, marking the strongest September for UK car manufacturing since 2023. The European Union remained the largest global destination, taking 57.5% of car shipments, with exports up 12.7% year on year. Shipments to the US rose 234.8%, while exports to China increased 357.7%, though from a low base. Despite the monthly rebound, total U.K. car and commercial vehicle production in the first nine months of the year fell 3% year on year to 564,537 units. The industry body reiterated concerns over the European Union’s proposed “Made in EU” measures and tougher post-Brexit rules of origin due to take effect from 2027, while warning that Britain’s electric-vehicle sales mandate is adding pressure on manufacturers and could threaten the sector’s recovery. “September’s rebound is welcome, but comparison with last year’s disruption masks the pressures on U.K. manufacturing,” said SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes. “Mandate targets are running ahead of demand and draining resources required for British factories and jobs.” An independent forecast cited by the SMMT expects U.K. light vehicle production to fall 2.3% to 731,000 units this year before recovering to 752,000 units in 2027 as new models, mostly electric vehicles, enter production. items.extracted_text: Argenta forecasts 18%+ returns at Lloyd’s in 2026, lower profits for 2027 amid softening - Artemis.bm Argenta forecasts 18%+ returns at Lloyd’s in 2026, lower profits for 2027 amid softening - Artemis.bm Argenta forecasts 18%+ returns at Lloyd’s in 2026, lower profits for 2027 amid softening 3rd November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard A new report published by Argenta Private Capital Limited (APCL) estimates a return on capital of more than 18% for its clients investing in the Lloyd’s of London market for 2026, but emphasises that profits are expected to narrow heading into 2027 as rates continue to soften. Argenta Private Capital underlined that insurance pricing has passed its recent peak, with rates softening in several areas as competition grows. Nevertheless, the firm acknowledges that demand in the Lloyd’s market remains strong and believes Lloyd’s can continue to deliver attractive returns, supported by prudent reserves, disciplined underwriting, and investment income. In the report, APCL reviewed current market conditions, syndicate business plans, and historical pricing trends for its clients. Reflecting current trading conditions, Argenta highlighted ongoing activity in the annual capacity auctions. “Lloyd’s capacity auctions began on 21 October 2026 and run for three consecutive weeks, allowing investors to purchase the right to support syndicates’ underwriting for the following year. Trading volumes for 2027 have so far been high, with the first auction seeing the largest volume traded in over twenty years. However, average capacity prices have been lower than last year, partly reflecting significant trading activity in lower-valued syndicates,” Argenta’s report reads. In view of this, selectivity becomes increasingly important, all of which leads Argenta to underline that investors should consider syndicate quality, business plans and capacity pricing alongside the role each syndicate plays within their wider portfolio. As profit margins also narrow, APCL stresses that careful syndicate selection becomes increasingly important. While estimating possible returns on capital for APCL advised clients, the company highlights that expected returns have gradually moderated from their 2023 peak, when APCL-advised clients achieved an average return on capital of 35%. “Our current estimated return for the 2024 year of account is 24.9%, while the early estimate for 2025 is around 28%. The higher 2025 figure reflects the relatively low level of catastrophe losses to date and takes into account that some 2025 polices might still be on risk. Both estimates may change as claims develop and syndicates adjust the funds they hold for future claims,” Argenta explains. Early signs for 2026 also appear encouraging, with APCL Research estimating a return on capital of over 18%, supported by low catastrophe losses and the tailwinds of strong historical pricing. But, looking ahead to 2027, the firm expects lower profitability across the market. “The broad picture is clear, although conditions vary by class of business. Prices are falling, profit margins are narrowing and planned combined ratios for 2027 are the weakest since 2019. This is not a cause for alarm, but it does mean that the realism of each plan and management’s ability to deliver against it warrant closer scrutiny,” the report reads. Moreover, APCL highlights how the property re/insurance market has experienced the steepest decline in pricing throughout 2026. In contrast, the firm notes that some syndicates see opportunities for growth within political risk, specialist reinsurance, and delegated authority business, where approved third-parties underwrite or distribute policies on behalf of the syndicate. When analysing the 2027 business plans of syndicates within APCL’s assessed cohort, the report reveals that the plans point to lower profits in several areas, with the clearest deterioration being displayed across non-marine reinsurance and direct and facultative property, where each risk is assessed and underwritten separately rather than as part of a wider treaty arrangement. At the same time, motor and portfolio solutions are also under pressure, with planned combined ratios above Lloyd’s 95% long-term benchmark. “For investors, the key message is that broad market strength is giving way to a more selective phase of the cycle,” APCL said. To conclude, Argenta outlines that competition is stronger across the market than it has been in recent years but emphasised that falling rates do not eliminate the investment case for Lloyd’s. The firm also added that prudent reserves, disciplined underwriting, and investment income can still support attractive returns where plans are realistic, and management teams execute them effectively. “The key change is increased differentiation. Variations in syndicate results are, in our opinion, likely to depend less on overall market strength and more on the quality of each syndicate and the realism of its plan. “A strong rating remains valuable, but it should always be considered alongside price and portfolio fit. APCL’s approach for 2027 is therefore selective. We favour syndicates with credible assumptions, disciplined management, and a clear role within a diversified portfolio, while remaining alert to relative value in capacity auctions and carefully selected new opportunities,” APCL concludes. items.extracted_text: NN Group sponsoring fourth Orange Capital Re cat bond, seeking €75m reinsurance - Artemis.bm NN Group sponsoring fourth Orange Capital Re cat bond, seeking €75m reinsurance - Artemis.bm NN Group sponsoring fourth Orange Capital Re cat bond, seeking €75m reinsurance 3rd November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans NN Group, or Nationale-Nederlanden, has returned to the catastrophe bond market with a target to secure €75 million or more in collateralised reinsurance to cover European perils through sponsorship of an Orange Capital Re DAC (Series 2026-1) offering, Artemis has learned. This is the fourth catastrophe bond sponsorship from NN Group, with all of its cat bond deals being under the Orange Capital DAC structure. NN Group first entered the catastrophe bond market in 2021, securing €75 million in collateralised European windstorm and severe thunderstorm catastrophe reinsurance with its debut Orange Capital Re DAC 2021-1 issuance The company added a second cat bond in 2023, securing a further €75 million of reinsurance coverage with the Orange Capital Re DAC (Series 2023-1) issuance, that sat lower down in its reinsurance tower. NN Group returned in 2024 and secured a renewal of the 2021 cat bond, with another €75 million of collateralised reinsurance from a Orange Capital Re DAC (Series 2024-1) deal. Now, the insurance group has returned again and this time it looks like the new cat bond is destined to at least in part act as a renewal of the 2023-1 issuance, whose coverage matures at the end of this year. NN Group is a life and property-casualty insurance underwriter based in the Netherlands, underwriting its risks largely in that country and some others close to it. NN Group is for the fourth time using Ireland as the domicile to issue its latest catastrophe bond, making use of the Orange Capital Re Designated Activity Company (DAC) for this Series 2026-1 cat bond issuance. It’s a similar transaction to all of the previous Orange Capital Re catastrophe bonds, in seeking a multi-year source of protection against losses from European windstorms and severe thunderstorms, sources explained. Orange Capital Re DAC is targeting issuance of a single tranche of €75 million or more Series 2026-1 Class A catastrophe bond notes. The notes will be sold to investors and the collateral will be used to underpin a catastrophe reinsurance arrangement covering windstorm and severe thunderstorm risks in Belgium and the Netherlands, we understand. As with the other Orange Capital Re cat bonds, the biggest exposure is to loss events impacting the Netherlands with this deal, given that is NN Group’s main underwriting market. The reinsurance protection will be structured on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis, running across a four year term, from January 2027 to the end of 2030. This is now the second four-year cat bond from NN Group, as prior to the 2024 deal the first two had three year terms. The ceding entity to this Orange Capital Re 2026-1 cat bond is NN Re, the Nationale-Nederlanden internal reinsurance vehicle that helps NN Group manage its risks, hedge its portfolio and also access private reinsurance markets, which has also been the cedent in the group’s previous cat bonds. The reinsurance agreement will be between the issuer Orange Capital RE DAC and NN Re, while NN Re then reinsures NN Group entities. We understand that the €75 million of Orange Capital Re Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes will have an initial attachment point at €300 million of losses, providing their coverage up to exhaustion at €400 million, suggesting some room to upsize the issuance should the sponsor choose to do so. The Series 2026-1 Class A notes issued by Orange Capital Re DAC will have an initial attachment probability of 5.07%, an initial expected loss of 4.24%, and are being offered to cat bond investors with spread price guidance in a range from 5.5% to 6%, sources told us. We can compare the price indications to the 2024-1 cat bond, but bearing in mind the reinsurance market was in a much harder pricing state at the time and there have also been risk model updates since, we understand. The Orange Capital Re 2024-1 cat bond had an initial expected loss of 2.7% and priced to pay investors a spread of 6%, so a much higher multiple-at-market than this new deal offers. As we said, it can be challenging to compare and we understand the European windstorm model has been updated since the 2024 deal. But, like every other recent catastrophe bonds, pricing is considerably lower than a comparable issuance in 2024 would have been. It’s good to see NN Group returning again and looking to layer more catastrophe bond protection within its reinsurance tower. You can read all about the Orange Capital Re DAC (Series 2026-1) catastrophe bond and every cat bond deal ever issued in our Artemis Deal Directory .
